---
title: "Comparing tests"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

A step test is most useful the second time: did the athlete improve, by how much, and is that more than the noise
of the test? This article uses the six tests of one trained cyclist in `lactate_tests` (real data from Trinity
College Dublin, CC BY 4.0), over five and a half years.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)

series <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(athlete == "cyclist_series")
series |>
  distinct(test, day)

analyse <- function(d) {
  series |>
    filter(day == d) |>
    lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE)
}
before <- analyse(0)
after <- analyse(58)
```

Before comparing, check both tests on their own (see [Checking the analysis](checking.html)), and make sure they
were run the same way: the same protocol, sampling site, sample type and analyzer (see [Best
practices](best-practices.html)).

## Is the change real?

A threshold moves between two tests even when fitness does not, through day-to-day variation and the error of the
analyzer and the method. `compare_tests()` gives every change an interval from the test-retest variation of the
method ([Hopkins, 2000](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200030010-00001); [Swinton et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2018.00041)) and calls it an increase or a decrease only when the whole interval is
on one side of zero, or of the smallest worthwhile change you set with `swc`.

```{r}
comparison <- compare_tests(before, after)
comparison |>
  select(method, before, after, change, change_low, change_high, verdict)
```

The default test-retest variation comes from trained male cyclists ([Heuberger et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846); [Pallares et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0163389))
and exists only for some methods; the others get a verdict once you give their `cv`, best measured on your own
athletes with your own protocol. `attr(comparison, "notes")` lists what could make two tests hard to compare: a
different protocol, sample type or resting sample, or a fall in peak lactate, which also moves the curve to the
right.

## How far did the curve move?

Thresholds are single points; the whole curve tells more. `curve_shift()` gives the intensity gained at each lactate,
and the lactate saved at the intensities you choose.

```{r}
curve_shift(before, after, intensity = c(250, 300))
autoplot(comparison)
```

## Did the curve shift, or change its shape?

Training can move the whole curve to the right, or change its shape: a later or a gentler rise. `curve_shape()`
fits both tests with the exponential plus constant, `lactate = a + b * exp(c * intensity)` ([Hughson et al., 1987](https://doi.org/10.1152/jappl.1987.62.5.1975)),
twice: once with one shape for both tests, the second moved sideways by a shift, and once with a shape for each
test. An extra-sum-of-squares F test and AICc compare the two fits ([Motulsky & Ransnas, 1987](https://doi.org/10.1096/fasebj.1.5.3315805)), and the shift comes
with a confidence interval.

```{r}
shape <- curve_shape(before, after)
shape
autoplot(shape)
```

In the first 58 days the curve moved by about 24 W, and one shape describes both tests. Five and a half years later,
it is a different story:

```{r}
later <- curve_shape(before, analyse(2046))
later
autoplot(later)
```

Read the result with care:

* **Little power.** With 6 to 10 stages per test, the F test has little power: "no evidence the shape changed" is
  not proof that it did not.
* **A shift is not always fitness.** In this model, a shift to the right is the same as a proportional fall of
  lactate above baseline. Better endurance, low glycogen stores and overreaching can all produce it ([Maassen & Busse,
  1989](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00637384); [Faude et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003)), so check the peak lactate, the diet before the test and the performance too.
* **The curve must fit.** The exponential cannot follow an early lactate dip; check both tests with
  `lactate_diagnostics()` first.

## A series of tests

For up to five tests, the plot of `lactate_trend()` shows where the curve moved and what that did to the training
zones: every lactate curve, light to dark by date, above the five zones of each test from the LT1 and LT2 you
choose. `day` takes the date of each test, or the days since the first. The test dates are not in `lactate_tests`, so
this example starts on a made-up date, with five of the six tests:

```{r, fig.height = 6}
days <- c(0, 163, 1107, 1865, 2046)
tests <- purrr::map(days, analyse)
trend <- lactate_trend(!!!tests, day = as.Date("2019-01-14") + days)
autoplot(trend, lt1 = "Bsln + 0.5", lt2 = "ModDmax")
```

The curve did not move in a straight line: in the third test, three years in, both thresholds sat below those of the
first test, with a higher peak lactate at the same peak power. `lactate_trend()` also fits a straight line to each
threshold, with its 90% interval, to show the direction without reading too much into one test ([Hopkins,
2017](https://www.sportsci.org/2017/wghtrend.htm)):

```{r}
trend |>
  filter(method %in% c("Bsln + 0.5", "ModDmax", "OBLA 4.0", "IAT"))
```

For longer series, such as monitoring over a season, the plot shows each threshold over time instead (`view =
"thresholds"`, the default above five tests): each test as a dot, against a gray band for the noise of the method
around the first test, where 90% of test-to-test changes fall when nothing changed ([Hopkins,
2000](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200030010-00001)).

To report a series to the athlete or the coach, give `test_report()` two to five tests and their dates: the report
starts with the progress, then describes the latest test ([see an
example](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/report-series-example.html)).

## Comparing athletes

Per kg of body mass, and as a percentage of the highest intensity and heart rate of the test:

```{r}
body_mass <- series |>
  filter(day == 58) |>
  pull(body_mass) |>
  first()

relative_thresholds(after, body_mass = body_mass) |>
  filter(method %in% c("Log-log", "ModDmax", "IAT")) |>
  select(method, intensity, intensity_per_kg, percent_peak, percent_peak_heart_rate)
```

A fixed lactate concentration falls at a similar percentage of peak power in trained and untrained people ([Maassen &
Busse, 1989](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00637384)), so a percentage of peak does not rank fitness on its own.
